On load and scroll no frame-to-frame change was detected in the first screen at 1440. With reducedMotion 'reduce' the first screen also showed no change.
observations.accessibility: Greyed employer logos and small check-marked terms are low contrast on the pale ground. App mockup text inside the scenario panels is very small at both widths. On mobile the main buttons are full width and well over 44px tall, but scenario tabs are clipped at the right edge of their row. No horizontal page overflow at 1440 or 390.
observations.mobile: At 390 the nav keeps the logo, a compact orange 'Create a workspace' button and a menu icon. Floating app icons gather into a single row above the h1, which drops to a measured 35.1px over three lines. 'Works with' logos form a 3×2 grid, buttons go full width, the app directory list is dropped in favour of Docs/Sheets/Slides pills over the preview, and scenario tabs scroll horizontally.
observations.copy: H1: "The Workspace Built For Human-AI Collaboration."; primary action "Create a workspace" (secondary "Invite your agent"). First-screen proof is the a16z Speedrun backing line, compatibility logos for agent tools and three plan terms (free up to 5 members, 1,000 AI actions a month, sign up in under 60 seconds).

principles: Give the agent its own entry point beside the human one ('Invite your agent' next to 'Create a workspace') when agents are first-class users.
Show the same action twice, as UI the team sees and as the code the agent runs, to prove an API-parity claim in one glance.
Name scenario tabs as concrete jobs ('Redline a contract', 'Triage your inbox') instead of feature names.
Put the price comparison against the stack being replaced in the page body when the product's pitch is consolidation.
interpretation.fit: Suits horizontal productivity suites and agent platforms where breadth and agent compatibility are the differentiators. It would be wrong for a single-purpose tool, where 18 apps and many tabs would dilute one clear job.
interpretation.risks: Inter in bold Title Case with a blue accent word reads as a common AI-startup default. Breadth (18 apps, many tabs) risks diluting the core claim, the mockups are too small to read on phones, and the employer-logo row signals founders' backgrounds rather than customers, which a visitor could misread.

limitations: The scenario panel may play a scripted sequence after a tab switch; only one frame 1.5s after the click was captured.
Pricing figures and testimonial metrics were not independently verified.
Mobile 'animations_on_load' measured 6 running animations; what moved at 390 was not observed live.
Single browser, single inspection date; homepage content can change.

name: Finni Health
summary: A fox mascot, blob-shaped photo frames and saturated orange, violet and green bands make an autism-care service feel warm, while a zip-code match field sits above the headline.

observations.hero: On a light grey ground, the left column stacks an orange kicker ('Navigating Autism, Together'), a short dark line about 1,000+ families in 25+ states, a zip-code field with an orange 'Find a match' button, and then the large violet h1. The right column holds a family photo in a rounded diamond frame with a white pill of three checks (insurance, HIPAA, families helped). A white 'We accept most insurance' bar with payer logos sits on an orange arc at the fold.
observations.typography: Measured h1: Outfit, 56px, weight 700, tracking 0, line-height 1.1, in violet. Measured body: General Sans, 16px, line-height 1.3, 83ch measure; Switzer also present. Section headings use the same rounded geometric sans in orange with a violet second clause; small outlined pill labels ('Provider-Led Care', 'The Finni Match') act as kickers.
observations.visual_system: Full-width bands of orange, violet, light grey, grass green and near-black. A cartoon fox mascot recurs across sections, alongside illustrated scenes (bedtime, a flower-and-bush hill) and white blob shapes holding statistics. Photography of children and families appears in rounded cards. Coloured tag chips list support areas. Orange is the action colour throughout.
observations.page_sequence: Hero with zip match → insurance logo bar → orange 'Finni providers are the best in the business' stat blobs → violet 'big feelings... big results' outcome cards with photos → three-step intake process → 'takes the weight off autism care' illustrated card with support tags → 'Snug as a glove' therapist profile and accordion → Parent Portal tabs (Scheduling, Progress Tracking, Insurance Management) → green testimonial → dark FAQ and contact → 'Find a provider with Finni Today' zip CTA → orange footer with state links.
observations.interaction: Operated the 'Progress Tracking' tab: the active pill turned orange and the carousel slid from the violet 'Shared Calendar and Scheduling' card to an orange 'Progress Tracking' card with a phone mockup showing '7 of 9 Treatment Goals Mastered' and a bar chart. On load the insurance logo row scrolls horizontally; with reducedMotion 'reduce' it still moved.
observations.accessibility: White body text on orange and violet bands and orange text on light grey look low contrast. Stat text inside the blobs is small and orange-on-white. The logo row keeps moving under reduced motion. The zip field relies on placeholder text ('Enter Zip Code') with no visible label. On mobile the 'Find a match' button appears about 40px tall. No horizontal overflow.
observations.mobile: At 390 the photo moves above the copy, everything centres, and the h1 drops to a measured 36px and sits below the zip form. The nav keeps the logo, an orange 'Get Started' pill and a menu icon. The three stat blobs stack vertically, outcome cards become a horizontal strip, and the page is 10,810px tall.
observations.copy: H1: "Finni Delivers Expert ABA & Mental Health Care Nationwide"; primary action "Find a match" (nav: "Get Started"). First-screen proof is the '1,000+ families in over 25 states' line, the insurance/HIPAA/families check pill and a row of insurer logos (Medicaid, UnitedHealthcare, Aetna, Kaiser Permanente, Anthem, Cigna, Optum).

principles: When the first question a visitor has is 'is this available to me?', put the eligibility input (a zip code) in the first screen ahead of the headline.
Show the payer or partner logos that decide whether a customer can buy, not just brand-name customers, directly under the hero.
A recurring mascot can soften a clinical, anxious decision and give long pages a consistent thread between sections.
Preview the logged-in product (a parent portal) with tabbed phone mockups so post-purchase experience becomes part of the pitch.
interpretation.fit: Suits consumer-facing healthcare, childcare and family services where trust, warmth and coverage matter more than technical depth. It would be wrong for a clinical B2B tool sold to health systems, where cartoon motifs could undercut perceived rigour.
interpretation.risks: The zip field sits above the h1, so the reading order puts the action before the claim. Outcome ranges (40-50%, 30-40%) carry no stated method. Many saturated bands and white-on-orange text weaken contrast, and the logo marquee ignores reduced motion. A large dark band near the FAQ rendered mostly empty in captures.

limitations: The zip-code match form was not submitted, so the matching flow is unverified.
Measurement reports no sticky nav, but during the live scroll the nav stayed at the top; the discrepancy was not resolved.
The dark band near the FAQ showed only the phrase 'long wait lists' in the full-page capture; its intended content was not seen.
Single browser, single inspection date; homepage content can change.

name: Meuze
summary: A dark halftone restaurant hero pinned through a long scroll track hands off to scroll-driven scenes that stage forecasting, stock, labor and ordering with illustrative mock data.

observations.hero: Full-bleed dark, dot-screened (halftone) image of an empty quick-service dining room with menu boards fills the first screen. A two-line headline sits left of centre, a two-sentence description and a blue 'Book a Demo' button sit bottom-left, and a hairline rule captioned 'Live data, every shift' sits bottom-right. The nav carries four uppercase links and a blue 'See it Live' button.
observations.typography: Measured h1: geist 47px, weight 300, tracking -0.025em, line-height 1.1, a light grotesque in title case (29.6px, -0.03em at 390). Section headlines switch to a book serif (measured families include lora) at a similar scale. Eyebrows and chart labels are tracked uppercase mono (measured family jetbrainsMono). Body: geist 15.5px/1.5, 53ch measure.
observations.visual_system: Near-black ground for hero, the scale band and the onboarding band; white panels framed by grey hairlines with small black square corner markers elsewhere. One saturated blue carries CTAs, active states and chart lines. Nearly all imagery is dot-matrix or halftone: the hero photo, an isometric store cutaway, a counter-scene illustration, a dotted globe and a large pixelated logo mark. Charts are small, light-grey and dotted.
observations.page_sequence: Hero (pinned ~4,050px scroll track) → How it works (four steps beside an isometric store) → Operations (four mini-dashboards: demand, ordering, labor, supply chain, plus integration marks) → Built for scale ('2,000+' over a globe, dark) → Forecast (scenario illustration with five metric tiles) → Any device (app icon) → Forward deployed (four onboarding steps, dark) → blue closing CTA band → footer.
observations.interaction: Clicked the 'Inventory' step in How it works: it turned blue, the page jumped ~1,460px down its track, and the store cutaway redrew with the dining room faded to dotted outline. On scroll, hero text dims to transparent and returns on scroll-up; Operations cards and onboarding steps light up in turn; the forecast scene swaps from a light weekday (740 guests) to a crowded night (2,220). Under reduced motion, no animations ran, nothing was hidden, the hero track collapsed, Operations cards and onboarding steps showed fully lit, and the forecast showed its night state.
observations.accessibility: No horizontal overflow at either width. Inactive steps and not-yet-reached Operations cards render as pale grey text on white, low contrast until activated. Mono micro-labels on charts and metric tiles are very small. At 390, footer links measure 19px tall and the scenario buttons 36px. The menu button has an aria-label, the globe's 23 site markers are labelled buttons (24×24), and a skip link exists. The hero video did not decode in the test browser; only its poster showed.
observations.mobile: Nav collapses to logo plus hamburger; 'See it Live' leaves the first screen. Hero recomposes: image band on top, headline (29.6px) beneath, description cut to its first sentence, 'Live data, every shift' caption gone. How it works becomes illustration, then active description, then a 2×2 tab grid. Operations cards stack full-width, all rendered fully. Forecast gains two visible buttons, 'Tue · Rain' and 'Sat · Match night', above five metric tiles in two columns. Page height drops from 19,710px to 10,389px.
observations.copy: H1: "The Company Brain For Your QSR Business."; primary action "Book a Demo" (nav: "See it Live"). The first screen offers no proof beyond the description; further down the page claims '2,000+ QSR locations running on Meuze' and shows five small grey integration marks (one legible as a Sysco wordmark) labelled 'Plus any system you run'.

principles: Show each capability as a tiny, specific operational artifact (a forecast curve with a 'match day' spike, a 'Pull 12kg, today 14:00' card) instead of a feature icon and a paragraph.
Keep one image treatment (halftone and dot-matrix) across photo, illustration, data and logo, so very different content reads as one system.
Pair a scroll-staged scenario with explicit buttons, as the mobile forecast does, so the comparison stays reachable without scrubbing.
Design the reduced-motion version as a complete static page: collapse scroll tracks and show every scene in its finished state rather than just stopping motion.
interpretation.fit: Suits operations or vertical-SaaS products whose value is a chain of decisions a buyer can picture in their own location (forecast, staff, order). Wrong for a self-serve developer tool where visitors want docs, pricing or a signup within one screen.
interpretation.risks: At desktop the hero sits in a ~4,050px scroll track (about four and a half viewport heights) before the first explanation arrives, and a static or non-JS capture shows thousands of pixels of empty dark band. Content is dimmed until scrolled into view, and on desktop the forecast comparison is bound to scroll rather than a control. Proof rests on one unattributed count and five small marks, and the first screen offers none.

limitations: The hero video (mp4) failed to decode in the test Chromium (no H.264), so the scroll-scrubbed footage was never seen; only the poster and the text fade were observed.
The desktop full-page screenshot was capped at 9,000px of a 19,710px page; the lower desktop sections were checked through live viewport captures only.
Desktop has no visible forecast switch (a 'Sat · Match night' button exists in the DOM but has zero size at 1440); the mobile scenario buttons were observed but not clicked.
Hover changes and the logo-mark pulse come from the measurement record, not from visual inspection; whether the globe rotates was not confirmed.
Only the homepage was visited; nav and footer destinations were not followed, and the '2,000+' figure and integration marks are recorded as page claims, not verified.
Single browser, single inspection date; homepage content can change.
Selected as a maintainer pick; no public design recognition was found and recorded.
The site's robots.txt allows the homepage and a few named pages only; nothing else on the domain was visited.
